hook.line: Move every piece into your rival’s corner to win. No captures — a quiet race.
hook.say: Let me show you the story of ugolki.

ch.say: All you need is a checkers board!
p: “Ugolki” is Russian for “corners”. Played with a checkers set, it has long been a children’s favourite across the former Soviet Union.
Its origin is unclear — some say late-18th-century Europe — and it closely resembles America’s Halma.

tl: One theory of a European origin
Halma is invented in the USA
“Stern-Halma” on a star board appears in Germany
Sold in the USA as “Chinese Checkers”
Ugolki is widely played in Russia and the USSR

ch.say: Your own pieces are springboards too!
ch.cap: A 3×4 formation; jump over pieces to advance
p: A piece steps one square or jumps over a neighbouring piece.
Jumps can be chained as often as you like — building a “road” with your own pieces is the key.

cards: 16×16 board; with two players, 19 pieces each race corner to corner
Played on a six-pointed star; a favourite in Japan as the “Diamond Game”
A version with a square block of 16 pieces

ch.say: There’s a secret hidden in the names.
stats: It uses a plain checkers board
cards: Taken from a Greek word meaning “jump”
Not from China at all — the name was given when Germany’s star-shaped Halma was sold in America

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: No — jumped pieces stay on the board
Many rule sets make you lose if you never leave your corner

p: Reach the far corner even one move faster than your rival.
